newsitem.title: FINLAND: World suffering diabetes epidemic, conference told.
newsitem.headline: World suffering diabetes epidemic, conference told.

text.p: Diabetes, already the fourth main cause of death in many countries, is becoming a truly global epidemic, experts told a conference on Monday.
Drug therapy for the potentially deadly illness has improved little since insulin injections were developed in 1922 and the best hope is to change the way people live, they said.

Diabetes affects 135 million people worldwide. By 2025, the World Health Organisation predicts, that number will reach 300 million. The rate is set to rise by 45 percent in developed countries and to triple in developing countries.
"I think we can truly say that the epidemic is here and now," Paul Zimmet, Chief Executive Officer of the International Diabetes Institute, told a news conference.
"Unless we do something dramatic, I expect diabetes to be one of the major killers in the world in the year 2010," agreed Jak Jervell, president of the International Diabetes Federation.
"What is bothering me is that developing countries will bear the brunt of this epidemic," he told the 9,000 delegates to the 16th International Diabetes Congress.

Jervell said complications from diabetes killed 2.8 million people around the world every year. About 10 percent of victims have type-one or insulin-dependent diabetes, which is often genetic in origin. The rest have type-two or non-insulin-dependent diabetes (NIDDM).
It kills by causing heart disease or kidney failure, and if untreated or poorly treated can cause blindness, vascular problems that lead to damage of the limbs, and other complications.

Zimmet said up to half of all people with diabetes did not even know they had it. Symptoms are vague -- tiredness, thirst and a need to urinate frequently are common as the body tries to flush away excess blood sugar that builds up as the pancreas fails to produce insulin.
By the time damage to tissue and blood vessels that marks the disease shows up, it can be too late.
People who were not at risk before were now getting diabetes, the experts said. While diabetes used to hit mostly those over the age of 50, cases were now common among people in their 20s and 30s.
Hilary King of the World Health Organisation said while most victims in developed countries were over 65, most in developing countries were aged 45 to 64.
"Clearly, we are not dealing with a geriatric disease here," he told a news conference.
Rates are skyrocketing in populations that are suddenly becoming modern and Westernised, such as Australian aborigines, Pacific islanders, native Americans and even among black children.
"The majority of new cases will be of type-two diabetes and will be in China, the Indian subcontinent and Africa," Zimmet said.
King agreed. "The pattern is a fairly severe and alarming one," he told a news conference.
The traditional medical approach of controlling diabetes with a low-fat, low-sugar diet, moderate exercise, and careful monitoring did not work with these new populations.
"They think their diabetes is due to the fact that the white man has taken away their lifestyle," Zimmet said.

King said the pattern of diabetes was going "hand-in-hand" with increasing obesity. All experts agree that as people switch to high-fat and high-sugar diets, bodies that evolved to respond to famine fail to handle the overload.
King, Zimmet and other experts said while drugs were useful for treating the symptoms of diabetes, they offered no cure. Eating habits and exercise were more important.
Although this sounded like a matter of individual responsibility, it was up to governments and society to make the needed changes.
"It's not enough simply to tell people what to eat and to exercise," King said. "You have to make it feasible for them."
